section.title: Steve Huynh: Amazon Promotions, Layoffs, and Interview Packaging
section.deck: Steve Huynh explains how a non-CS path led into Amazon, why behavioral fit shapes big-tech interview levels, and how promotion and managed-out cycles work.

blocks.text: Steve Huynh's view is that a big-tech interview is mainly a test of fit. Coding and system design rounds work as a pass or fail filter, and behavioral answers shape the level a candidate is offered. Steve applies the same idea to careers: ask directly what the expectations are, raise bad news early, and close gaps in a promotion packet rather than repeating strengths. Steve credits Amazon's customer focus and writing culture as real strengths, and says its managed-out cycles are hard to watch and have become more of a mandate. These are Steve's own views and experience, not verified facts. Editorial note: the host is not named in the transcript, so the host appears only as the host.
blocks.heading: Steve's view: big-tech interviews judge fit, and promotion depends on early, explicit feedback

blocks.question: How did someone with a liberal arts degree and no computer science major get into Amazon?
answer: Steve says the liberal arts label is somewhat misleading. Both parents were electrical engineers, and a family computer was always around. Steve programmed from a young age, took the high school AP computer science exams, and built a Tetris clone.

In college Steve earned a liberal arts degree, a minor in math and applied math, and some computer science courses. After graduating, Steve wanted to be a writer, but a writing professor said there was no job called writer. Steve went back to the programming skills from high school instead. Steve agrees that an English major alone would not stand out to a recruiter.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How did Steve get the first job at Amazon?
answer: Steve says it came through networking. A high school AP computer science classmate had earned a degree and worked as an Amazon software developer. The team needed support engineers, and the classmate helped Steve get an interview for a contract role.

Steve says the support work involved scripts and maintaining systems, so the coding interview was not a worry. Steve was a green badge contractor, Amazon's term for a temp, for about nine months before moving to a full-time blue badge role.

followups.question: Did a referral matter more than skills in getting hired?
answer: Steve says both matter. Opportunity arrives unevenly, so a referral from a friend or relative can open a door. Preparation is the part a person controls. Steve says the two have to meet, because an opening is wasted without the skills to fill it.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Was it harder to break into tech before interview prep became a large industry?
answer: Steve says yes. There were no widely shared lists of LeetCode questions when Steve was trying to get in, so a non-traditional candidate had a harder time than today. Steve does not say that getting in is easy now.

As a support engineer who wanted to be a software developer, Steve collected interview questions from colleagues and asked them not to give the answers. Steve worked each problem in an IDE and wrote custom test cases, which Steve calls the old-fashioned way.

followups.question: Is interview prep a competition in which a candidate must beat the other candidates?
answer: Steve says yes and no. Demand for software developers is skewed toward senior roles, with little demand for junior engineers. Steve sees the competition at the selection stage, when recruiters screen candidates, not in the interview itself.
Steve says a candidate can stand out before the interview, through a contact at the company or by going deep in one area.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Why is most interview prep advice poor?
answer: Steve says most interview prep is not optimized. Candidates focus heavily on coding and, lately, on system design. Steve says prep turns the interview into a test. That view is partly right, since a candidate who cannot code or design a system is unlikely to be hired, but Steve says the focus is too narrow.

followups.question: What would a better balance of interview prep look like?
answer: Steve says an interview is more like a date than an SAT, because both sides are deciding whether they want to work together. Prep sources present it as a test because a test is easier to sell.

Steve suggests spending less time on coding and system design and more on behavioral work. A rough split Steve offers is 40 percent coding, 40 percent system design, and 20 percent behavioral. Steve treats the figures as an illustration, not a rule.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How much does the behavioral part of an interview count compared with coding and system design?
answer: Steve says coding and system design work like the small and big blinds in poker. They are required to play, but they do not decide the hand. The behavioral round decides the hand. Steve was a bar raiser trainer and trained thousands of Amazon interviewers. Steve says the functional rounds are pass or no pass.

Steve says Amazon will say no to candidates with poor behavioral answers, even when coding and system design are strong. That does not mean the candidate lacks experience. Interviewers can often see early that a candidate will not fit the company. Once a candidate passes, the behavioral answers shape the level.

followups.question: How can a candidate avoid being down-leveled because of weak behavioral answers?
answer: Steve recommends packaging: presenting one's experience as a clear story about what one has done, how one operates, and what one is about. The story does not have to be entertaining, but it should be efficient and honest.

Steve says the core question of an interview is whether the interviewer wants to work with the candidate. Good behavioral answers help the interviewer answer that. Candidates should not misrepresent themselves, but should put their best foot forward.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

followups.question: What does a packaged answer sound like?
answer: Steve gives an improvised example for a tell-me-about-yourself question: a focus on backend distributed systems, a love of customer-facing products, a sports interest, and experience building teams and improving engineering culture. Steve says many candidates rush through this question.
Steve says stories betray level. A story about an entry-level task sounds junior when the candidate is aiming for a senior role, and that mismatch can lead to being down-leveled.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Can someone's level be judged in a short conversation?
answer: The host suggests a blind test: talk to someone for five minutes and guess their level. Steve says Steve is fairly confident in judging level this way. A junior engineer usually shows it in how they carry themselves and what they talk about.
Steve says judging whether a strong senior engineer could pass as a principal would be harder. Steve believes Steve is well calibrated on level overall.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How can someone stand out before the interview, for example when seeking a referral?
answer: Steve says a direct, genuine message to someone on a team with an opening can work. Steve suggests saying you noticed their team has openings, and asking what their day-to-day work is like. The message should not look like spam, an automated DM, or AI-written text.

Steve cites a poll Steve ran in a Discord community. About 90 percent of respondents said they would engage with a genuine message like that, and would refer the sender if asked. Steve presents this as informal, not as evidence.
Steve says real networking means making a connection and offering value. Newcomers who are willing to pick up a useful skill are also more attractive to big tech.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Should a learner go deep or broad, and which language should they pick?
answer: Steve says most people should go deep rather than broad. Jumping between a React tutorial, Rust, and PyTorch creates no cohesion. Steve suggests starting with a framework or language the learner already knows and going as deep as possible.

Asked for a top language for 2025, Steve jokes that English is the top language. Steve says the high-leverage skill is communicating and packaging one's experience. Steve says languages come and go, and that Steve's own Perl expertise is no longer useful.
Steve says curiosity should guide the choice. Java is not going away, so becoming an expert in it is a fine choice even if it is not glamorous.

followups.question: What does going deep look like in practice?
answer: Steve gives the example of asking what a Java virtual machine does, what a garbage collector does, and what tuning one means. Steve notes that tuning garbage collection can backfire, but looking under the hood is something no one can stop a learner from doing.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Will AI take over junior engineering work? Meta's chief executive, called Zuck in the conversation, recently suggested AI could produce mid-level engineer code within the year.
answer: Steve says CEOs make predictions that tend to undershoot on timing and overshoot on ability, but that the vision is real. Steve reads the hedged wording about mid-level AI engineers later this year as a sign the rollout is further away than the words suggest. Steve says leaders' jobs are to move the goalposts a little past where things are.

Steve agrees that AI should take on some tasks. Steve compares it with older tools: code generation, Lombok annotations that remove getters and setters, and IDE refactoring. Steve calls AI help an amplifier.

followups.question: Can AI take a non-coder from idea to working product, and does that scale?
answer: Steve says AI can take a non-coder from zero to one very easily. Steve mentions app-building products that go from start to finish, but doubts they would handle an app that does not work as intended or must scale to a very large user base.
Steve believes an engineer can become much more productive with AI help today, moving from a 1x to a 10x engineer. Steve does not see a jump from zero to a 10x engineer happening later this year.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How did Steve move from support engineer to SDE1, SDE2, and SDE3?
answer: Steve says the path from support engineer to SDE3 took about three and a half years. At SDE1, the focus is independence: understanding where one's work fits in the development life cycle and taking tasks all the way through, so that the team trusts the person without hand-holding.

followups.question: Does independence mean never asking for help?
answer: Steve says no. Self-contained is not the same as independent. Steve says the real skill is knowing how to unblock oneself, and being comfortable asking questions and raising issues when stuck.
Steve warns that hiding problems becomes a performance issue. A two-week task reported as on track until the Thursday before it is due is more serious than a task that is merely slow.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

followups.question: What changes at SDE2?
answer: Steve says the key word at SDE2 is ownership. An SDE2 takes an active part in the development life cycle and acts as a steward of the team's codebase, cleaning up tech debt instead of leaving a mess. Steve likes the image of not littering, and sometimes picking up trash.

Steve says each step up is an argument for more scope. An SDE2 works at team level, understands the codebase's strengths and weaknesses, suggests where it should go, and takes on-call shifts. Steve calls this a meat-and-potatoes role, and says it is what a person needs to show to move from SDE2 to SDE3.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Can an SDE2 stay at that level for a whole career, or is it a terminal level at Amazon?
answer: Steve says this is debated at Amazon. Steve sees the SDE2 band as wide, and says many senior engineers at other companies would sit at the upper end of SDE2 at Amazon. Steve says SDE2 could be a terminal level, but Steve does not advise treating it as one.

followups.question: Is there an up-or-out policy?
answer: Steve says SDE1 is clearly up or out. Staying more than about two years brings progressively stronger guidance to move on, though it is not a fixed 24- or 36-month rule. Steve calls it a feel thing.

For SDE2, Steve says the answer depends on upper management and on the individual's manager. A manager who sees an SDE2 as overdue for promotion could make staying very hard. The conversation notes that many people worry Meta could become more like Amazon, which is known for intense performance management.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How many people is Amazon expected to cut each year?
answer: Steve will not give an exact number. Steve uses five or six percent as an example. For an organization, that figure used to be a soft recommendation to manage out part of the team over a year. In the past couple of years, Steve says it has become much more of a mandate.

Steve says the pressure grew when backfills were paused. Until recently, Amazon did not backfill many roles, so people felt chased from behind, and Steve does not think that was healthy. As a self-described high performer, Steve says it is hard to speak to what it feels like to fear losing a job.

followups.question: Is managing out the low end of the curve a relief or a problem?
answer: Steve uses a group of 20 people as an example. In normal years, people on the low end of the curve are often not thriving in Amazon's culture. Steve says removing them can feel like a relief, a blessing in disguise, because it ends a poor fit.
Steve is uncomfortable when cuts reach people in the middle of the curve, who would be fine in other years. Repeated cuts of about six percent, with no backfill, push out people who are doing well.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How do senior engineers take part in the meetings where people are discussed for being managed out?
answer: Steve says engineers are pulled into these discussions from senior engineer level, and definitely from L7 and above. The meetings can run three days, with people in a room discussing colleagues through measurable results and other people's feedback. Steve says some recent cuts of middle managers surprised Steve, since a 6 percent target makes little sense for a group of four or eight people.

Steve says the process is not linear. In a perfect world, each person would get equal time, but the discussion tends to focus on the edges, the strongest and the weakest. Steve sees this as a matter of the numbers, not a verdict on the decision makers, and says the process strips out some humanity. Steve says it is not a favorite time of year.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Is Meta showing the same intensity as Amazon?
answer: Steve says Meta appears to be on a hiring spree, and that a figure of about 5 percent of low performers has been floated around. Steve has a sense that people affected are not having a good time, but thinks most people at Meta are fine.
Steve says that with a large population, someone is always struggling. Meta's inflow of hires is far larger than its outflow, so Steve would not be too worried.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What protects someone who is meeting expectations during a cut cycle?
answer: Steve says solidly meeting expectations is the main protection. Steve does not think a 5 percent stack ranking should remove people who meet expectations, and Steve dislikes the label low performer. Steve describes it as a mismatch between a person and the culture around them, not a judgment of ability.

Steve says offers at Meta are hard to get, so the people in that process are not weak. Steve advises people labeled as low performers to find the specific dimension they are judged on, rather than trying to become high performers in general.

followups.question: What should someone do first when judged to be below expectations?
answer: Steve says to crawl before walking and running. Find out exactly what the judgment is about, then check with the manager whether expectations are being met. If they are not, propose a preemptive plan to get back to the median. Steve would avoid the phrase PIP, for performance improvement plan, when asking for one.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

followups.question: Should employees ask managers directly what the expectations are, and when should they report bad news?
answer: Steve says most people never ask this. Steve estimates that about 25 percent of software developers have explicitly asked their manager about expectations. Steve recommends asking directly what the expectations are, then asking whether one is meeting them.

Steve credits a friend with the saying that early bad news is just news, while late bad news is terrible news. Steve advises surfacing problems early in the review cycle, not in the month before a review, so there is time to fix them.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: How did Steve get principal-level scope at Amazon?
answer: Steve says a reorg moved Steve into Prime Video after a team Steve cared about, the Amazon Tickets team, was spun down and its developers scattered. Steve chose a Prime Video team focused on delivering live sports, then saw a large catalog project that principal engineers knew needed doing. Steve decided to take it on and stay on the team.

Steve says the work fell in the gaps between principal areas, such as playback, clients, or catalog. It needed an end-to-end solution, and the other principals were busy with their own areas. The host adds that delivering such work gives principal engineers context to champion the candidate in a promotion packet.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What usually blocks someone from going from senior to principal at Amazon?
answer: Steve says Amazon effectively skips a level, and that a staff level could be inserted between senior and principal. Steve says the jump from senior to principal is two levels, so the criteria roughly double. Influencing multiple teams makes it hard to show that in one year.

Steve sees a common failure. People think they are ready, push for promotion, get rejected, and go back to their strengths. Closing the feedback takes a long time, and many give up. Steve knows people who left Amazon and now work at senior staff or principal levels elsewhere, but could not make the jump there.

followups.question: How can someone get a low performance rating while doing principal-level work?
answer: Steve says performance and promotion are decoupled. Reviews run yearly, with a smaller check every six months, and promotion can happen quarterly or every six months. Steve describes an anti-pattern: a senior engineer who stops doing senior work and focuses only on principal-level work.

Steve says senior engineers must code. Principals also code, but less, and they do cross-functional work such as sponsoring projects, acting as a backstop, or evangelizing an initiative across several dev teams. Steve recalls a promotion review that said Steve acted like a TPM, and Steve took offense.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

followups.question: What feedback did Steve get on coding, and why?
answer: Steve says the review said to code more. Steve had checked in a lot of code, but in one six-month stretch Steve coded less, and the review looked only at the code delivered in that period. Steve says that gave no credit for time served.

Steve says on-call history was also raised, though Steve had been on call for years, including about four years in a row. Steve also says Steve reached senior in 2012 and principal in 2020, after the promotion process changed three times in four years.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What did Steve learn from becoming an expert in the promotion process?
answer: Steve says Steve did not get promoted through ability alone. Steve became an expert in the process of getting promoted, and thinks that skill is useful. Steve had not produced enough tangible evidence for the packet, and needed a manager's support. Steve says the process changed three times in four years.

Steve's first lesson is to start early. Many people wait until a big project lands, but the project landing is often not what a rejection is about. Steve advises submitting the packet early to get real feedback on the gaps.

Steve's second lesson concerns strengths. A packet gives some credit for strengths, but reviewers focus on the delta. Steve advises prioritizing weaknesses and gaps, and keeping strengths from regressing, the way a cook tends one pot of risotto while the other pans rest.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What are Steve's favorite parts of Amazon's culture?
answer: Steve says the biggest part is customer obsession. From interns to VPs, people were expected to put the customer first. Steve says working backward from the customer is the right North Star. Optimizing for short-term profit or for competitors can backfire, and Steve credits Jeff Bezos with the idea that long-term profit and customers are the same thing.

Steve calls the writing culture a superpower, and credits a writing background with making a six-page document easier to write. Meetings often begin with about 30 minutes of reading the document, followed by discussion. Steve says writing is learnable and need not be a focus before joining.

followups.question: What does Steve dislike about the culture?
answer: Steve says the inside joke among friends was frugality. Anything cheap or poor, such as the lack of free food or weak hardware, got the label. Steve says free food is a perk and its absence does not mean a company is bad, but frugality can go too far.

Steve recalls begging and pleading for a laptop with enough memory so the fan did not overheat while building code. Steve says a company hiring tens of thousands of developers should give them working computers, and recalls monitors being taken after intern season.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What made a good manager stand out, given the many managers Steve had?
answer: Steve says the count was more than 17, closer to the 20s. Steve says the best managers were personal, but Steve resonated with managers who reasoned from principles. Those managers treated the leadership principles as axioms, so decisions followed from them and had implications.

Steve says the best managers held firm on customer obsession and on thinking ahead. They would accept a short-term hack if it fit a future-facing choice. Steve found managers focused only on near-term delivery harder to work with. Steve also notes that some people who complain about micromanagers really need things broken down.

followups.question: Who were the worst managers, and what made them bad?
answer: Steve does not name names. Steve says the worst managers were a mix of style mismatch and a sense that the hiring and promotion processes should have filtered them out. A manager who is caring and engaged for one person may be a poor fit for another.
Steve says it was sometimes hard to see how some managers had reached their roles.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: Why did Steve stay at Amazon for 18 years?
answer: Steve says Amazon's size allowed many careers inside one company. Steve worked on the first Kindle, on a precursor to Prime Video, back on Prime Video, and in payments. Steve says it did not feel like one team for 18 years.

followups.question: Did Steve consider leaving, and what is the advice on job hopping?
answer: Steve says Steve considered leaving several times. Early in a career, job hopping makes sense to raise total pay, and Steve says that advice works until about the senior level.

Steve says distinguished, principal, and staff engineers at the top usually stayed on the same team, on the same problem, for at least three years and often about five. Steve's rule of thumb for a fast climb is to job hop every two years until about mid-level, then put down roots.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

followups.question: Why did Steve choose to put down roots?
answer: Steve says staying made sense without a computer science background. There was a lot to learn in large amounts of code, wikis, and internal videos. Steve felt Steve could grow the way Steve wanted by staying.
followups.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What is Steve's biggest career regret?
answer: Steve says the regret is not noticing a bad situation or team and making a clear decision about it. The default is to stay put, and deferring a decision turns into staying by default. Steve's advice is to weigh the considerations and then make the choice explicit.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh

blocks.question: What would Steve tell a younger self who had just finished college?
answer: Steve says Steve would warn against people pleasing. Steve describes a culture of tracks, such as school, then job, then marriage, and a sense of being ahead or behind. Steve also sought validation after each achievement, and doubts a younger self would have listened.

Steve says the person to please is oneself. Steve asks whether a person is doing what they want or what someone else expects, and whether they are climbing the ladder to reach the top or because it was put in front of them.
blocks.speaker: Steve Huynh
